# Lesson 3 · Groups and membership rules

=== "Theory"

    ## What an Okta group represents

    A **group** is a collection of user accounts in an org. **Membership** is the relationship between a particular user and that group. Open **Directory → Groups**, select a group, and open **People** to see that relationship from the group side.

    Why have a group? It gives an administrator one place to manage a set of users. If several users need the same application, you can assign the application to their group. If a sign-in policy has a rule meant for a particular set of users, it can use a group to identify them. The group holds the membership. The application or policy configuration decides what to do with it.

    | What you are looking at | What it tells you |
    | --- | --- |
    | A user's **Department** profile attribute | The department value stored on that user's Okta profile. |
    | A group's **People** tab | Which user accounts currently belong to the group. |
    | An app integration's **Assignments** tab | Which users or groups receive that app integration. |

    Those are separate records. A department value can exist even if no group rule reads it. Membership can exist even if the group has no applications assigned.

    ## Who manages the group?

    An **Okta group** is a group managed inside Okta. Administrators can create one and manage its members directly or use rules. An **imported group** comes from a connected directory or application. For example, a group imported from Active Directory represents a group that exists in AD. When AD owns the group's membership, start in AD to understand why a user belongs to it and check the import to see how that membership reached Okta. We'll practice the directory side later.

    **Everyone** is the built-in group that contains the org's users. Check the audience before assigning an app to it. **Okta Administrators** is another built-in group. Okta maintains its membership and uses it for sign-on policies. Its member count is hidden, and you cannot assign it to an app. We'll use separate groups for the exercises. [Okta · Groups](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/Content/Topics/users-groups-profiles/usgp-about-groups.htm)

    ### Find the right group and check its members

    **Directory → Groups** searches by the beginning of a name by default. If you remember only a word in the middle, try **Advanced Search → Contains** on the name or description. Give it at least three characters. To see how someone became a member, open the group and look for that person under **People**. A number in the Groups list may lag behind a membership change because it refreshes on a two-hour schedule. [Okta · Groups](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/Content/Topics/users-groups-profiles/usgp-about-groups.htm) · [Okta · View and edit group attributes](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/Content/Topics/users-groups-profiles/usgp-view-edit-group-attributes.htm) · [Okta · Verify membership](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/Content/Topics/users-groups-profiles/usgp-verify-group-membership.htm)

    ### Read imported membership one group at a time

    A **nested group** is a group placed inside another group. Okta does not store groups inside groups. When an import resolves nested directory membership, Okta represents the result as the user belonging to each applicable group. If you see two copies of a group name, check each group's source before changing a rule. For example, the same group can reach Okta through an AD import and through an Office 365 integration that also imports it. Use the group's ID when an expression needs to check one specific record. [Okta · Manage groups](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/Content/Topics/users-groups-profiles/usgp-groups-main.htm) · [Okta · Office 365 group duplication](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/Content/Topics/users-groups-profiles/usgp-group-duplication-365.htm)

    ## What a group rule does

    A **group rule** connects information Okta already has to a membership decision. Its **condition** is the question Okta asks about a user. Its **target group** is the group Okta should add the user to when the answer is true. An **exception** identifies a user the rule should skip.

    A condition can read a user attribute, check whether the user belongs to another group, or combine checks. If the original attribute comes from a connected source, the rule reads the corresponding value on the **Okta user profile**. Check the value in Okta first. If it is missing or wrong, trace the mapping or the source.

    ### Follow one membership change

    1. You save a rule. Okta creates it as **Inactive**. You can review its condition and target before it starts managing anyone.
    2. You activate the rule. Okta applies it across the org. A basic attribute rule evaluates eligible active users. Keep the condition narrow when you are testing.
    3. For each eligible user, Okta checks the value on that user's profile and compares it with the condition. If the value matches and the user is outside the exception list, the rule can add the user to the target group.
    4. A later profile change can trigger another evaluation. If a user no longer matches, Okta can remove the membership managed by that rule. When you test this, use a dedicated target group with only the one rule so the outcome is easy to trace.

    Check **Directory → Groups → Rules** for the configuration. Check the group's **People** tab for the result. A saved condition and a current membership answer different questions.

    ## Edit an active rule

    In **Directory → Groups → Rules**, open **Actions** for the rule. An active rule offers **View** so you can inspect its condition. Okta only enables **Edit** while the rule is inactive. The status you see here belongs to the rule itself.

    1. Select **Actions → Deactivate** and verify the rule shows **Inactive**.
    2. Select **Actions → Edit**. Change the condition, exceptions, or target groups as needed, then **Save**.
    3. Select **Actions → Activate** to run the saved rule again.
    4. After Okta processes the change, open the target group's **People** tab. Check a user who should now qualify and one who should stay outside the group.

    After you save and reactivate, Okta automatically updates group membership based on the edited settings. If a target group grants app access, also check its app assignments for the affected users. Use a dedicated lab group to practice the change. [Okta · Edit group rules](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/content/topics/users-groups-profiles/usgp-edit-group-rules.htm)

    **Deactivation keeps existing rule-managed members in the group.** It pauses rule processing. To understand what happens to access, check the group's current **People** list and the apps assigned to it. Deleting the rule is a separate operation. Its dialog gives you the choice to leave or remove the memberships the rule created. [Okta · Deactivating and deleting group rules](https://support.okta.com/help/s/article/what-happens-if-group-rules-are-deactivated-and-deleted)

    ## Manual membership and rule-managed membership

    An administrator can select a user and add them to an Okta group. The group can show that membership as **Manually** managed. When a rule manages the membership, the group can show the rule responsible for it.

    Manual and rule-managed members can be in the same group. Okta documents that a new rule can take over management of a manually added member who matches it. If an administrator manually removes a rule-managed member, Okta adds that user to the rule's exception list. That is why a matching profile value alone may fail to explain a missing membership.

    ## When to use an expression

    **Okta Expression Language** is how you write a condition directly when the basic controls do not express the check you need. A group rule expression must give Okta a **Boolean** result, meaning true or false.

    In `user.department == "Lab-Finance"`, `user.department` reads the Department value on the Okta user profile. The two equals signs compare that value with the text on the right. If the values match, the expression returns true. Read the condition aloud before saving it so you can predict who qualifies.

    ## How one group can add a user to two other groups

    Start with one test user and three groups you create under **Directory → Groups**.

    | Okta group | What you do with it |
    | --- | --- |
    | `LAB-Rule-Source` | Add the test user here yourself. This is the **source group**, the group Okta checks. |
    | `LAB-Rule-Target-A` | Leave this empty at first. This is the first **target group**, where the rule can add the user. |
    | `LAB-Rule-Target-B` | Leave this empty too. This is the second target group. |

    When you open **Directory → Groups → Rules → Add Rule**, read the form in two parts.

    1. Under **IF**, ask Okta, “Is this user in `LAB-Rule-Source`?”
    2. Under **Then Assign to**, select `LAB-Rule-Target-A` and `LAB-Rule-Target-B`. You are telling Okta, “If the answer is yes, add this user to both of these groups.”

    Once the rule is active and Okta processes the membership, open the **People** tab in each group. The same user should appear in all three. You added them to the source. The rule added them to the two targets.

    Now remove the user from the **source** group's **People** tab. When Okta checks again, the answer to **IF** is now no. In this lab, the rule was the user's only way into either target, so the user should disappear from both targets after Okta processes the change. If a target is missing a user you expected to see, start by checking the source membership. Then check that the rule is active, the intended target is selected, and the user is outside the exception list. [Okta · Create group rules](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/Content/Topics/users-groups-profiles/usgp-create-group-rules.htm)

    ### What changes when you add more groups?

    Adding a group under **IF** gives Okta another membership to check. Adding a group under **Then Assign to** gives a qualifying user another membership. You can check several sources and assign up to **100 targets per rule**. Everyone who qualifies for that rule gets every target you selected. If members of one source should get Target A and members of another source should get Target B, give each source its own rule and select its corresponding target. A user who matches both rules can get both targets. [Okta · Create group rules](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/Content/Topics/users-groups-profiles/usgp-create-group-rules.htm) · [Okta · Rule limits](https://support.okta.com/help/s/article/okta-group-rule-limitations-and-restrictions?language=en_US)

    ### With two source groups, who should get in?

    Keep `LAB-Rule-Source` and create another Okta group called `LAB-Rule-Source-B`. For the next few examples, **Source A** means `LAB-Rule-Source` and **Source B** means `LAB-Rule-Source-B`. The two target groups from above are still separate from these sources.

    Say the test user belongs only to Source A. Should they get both targets?

    - Choose **OR** if the answer is yes. One source membership is enough. A user who belongs to both also qualifies.
    - Choose **AND** if the answer is no. The user must belong to both sources before Okta adds them to the targets.

    | Where the user belongs | **Source A OR Source B** | **Source A AND Source B** |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Neither source | Does not qualify | Does not qualify |
    | Source A only | Qualifies | Does not qualify |
    | Source B only | Qualifies | Does not qualify |
    | Both sources | Qualifies | Qualifies |

    Picture the user starting in both sources. You remove them from Source A and leave them in Source B. With **OR**, they keep the target memberships because B still qualifies them. With **AND**, they lose the memberships this rule gave them because they need A as well.

    ### Where do you choose AND or OR in the console?

    **IF** is the section of the form. Inside it, you can choose **Use basic condition** or **Use Okta Expression Language (advanced)**.

    In **Use basic condition**, select **Group membership**. The words beside it say **includes any of the following**. That means **OR**. If you select Source A and Source B and your test user belongs only to Source A, **Preview** should show **User matches rule**. If you selected two target groups under **Then Assign to**, a matching user qualifies for both targets when the rule runs.

    If you need the user to belong to **both** source groups, choose **Use Okta Expression Language (advanced)** and join the two checks with `AND`. You can also write `OR` in the advanced editor if either source is enough. [Okta · Create group rules](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/Content/Topics/users-groups-profiles/usgp-create-group-rules.htm)

    First, get the **group ID** for each source. A group ID is the unique value Okta uses to identify exactly one group, even when group names repeat. Open each source under **Directory → Groups** and copy the ID at the end of the browser address. In the expressions below, replace `SOURCE_A_ID` and `SOURCE_B_ID` with what you copied. Keep the quotation marks. Each `isMemberOfGroup(...)` check asks, “Does the user belong to this group?” [Okta · Find the group ID](https://support.okta.com/help/s/article/how-to-find-group-ids-through-the-okta-user-interface) · [Okta · Group functions](https://developer.okta.com/docs/reference/okta-expression-language/#group-functions)

    | Who should qualify? | What to enter under **IF** |
    | --- | --- |
    | A member of either source | `isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_A_ID") OR isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_B_ID")` |
    | A member of both sources | `isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_A_ID") AND isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_B_ID")` |
    | A member of any source in a list | `isMemberOfAnyGroup("SOURCE_A_ID", "SOURCE_B_ID")` |

    The last row is another way to write **OR**. It is handy when you have a longer list of source groups.

    ### What if group membership is only part of the decision?

    **Check a profile field too.** Suppose either source is enough, but the user's Department also has to be `Lab-Finance`. Put the two group checks in parentheses. The parentheses make the Department requirement apply to users from either source.

    ```text
    (isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_A_ID") OR isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_B_ID")) AND user.department == "Lab-Finance"
    ```

    **Use a group to exclude people.** Suppose Source A qualifies a user, but anyone in Source B should be skipped. The `!` means **not**, so the condition asks for membership in A and no membership in B.

    ```text
    isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_A_ID") AND !isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_B_ID")
    ```

    **Skip a specific person.** Use **Except The following users** when you need to exclude someone by name. If you manually remove a user whose target membership came from this rule, Okta adds that user to the rule's exception list. Their source membership stays in place. If they still qualify and you expect them to rejoin, check the exception list. [Okta · Exclude groups from a rule](https://support.okta.com/help/s/article/How-to-exclude-specific-groups-in-group-rule?language=en_US) · [Okta · Create group rules](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/Content/Topics/users-groups-profiles/usgp-create-group-rules.htm)

    ### When can you keep it to one rule?

    Imagine one rule adds a user to Target A, and a second rule looks for membership in Target A before it adds them to Target B. The second rule has to wait for the first. Okta calls this a **cascading rule** and advises avoiding it because it can slow rule processing. If the same people should get both groups, use the original **IF** condition and select both groups under **Then Assign to**. Okta blocks group rules from assigning users to groups that grant Okta admin privileges. [Okta · Group rules best practices](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/Content/Topics/users-groups-profiles/usgp-group-rules-best.htm) · [Okta · Group rules](https://help.okta.com/okta_help.htm?id=ext_Group_Rules&type=oie)

    ## Check the user's status before debugging the expression

    Okta's rule documentation says that a rule with no explicit status condition includes active users. If you want the condition itself to check for that status, use `user.getInternalProperty("status") == "ACTIVE"`. Add it with `AND` when both the status and another condition must be true. A newly staged account can already have the correct Department and still be ineligible for an active-user rule.

    A rule condition must return true or false. Use `==` to compare values, `AND` when both checks must pass, and `OR` when either check is enough. You can reference attributes on the Okta user profile and supported group functions. If the data comes from a connected app or directory, map it into an Okta user attribute before using it in a group rule. Use the variable name from **Profile Editor** when writing the expression.

    **Preview before you activate.** An active rule can affect eligible users across the org. An **import safeguard** can block an import that would unassign too many users, but Okta says it does not trigger when a group rule reduces app membership. Test an expected match and an expected miss before changing a rule linked to app access. [Okta · Group rules best practices](https://help.okta.com/oie/en-us/Content/Topics/users-groups-profiles/usgp-group-rules-best.htm)

=== "Hands-on Lab"

    ## Lab 3 · Manage group membership

    === "1. Profiles and manual membership"

        Use the Integrator org and the two **Active** test users from Lesson 2. All changes in this lab apply to those test users and the groups you create here. Keep track of which account you use first and which you use second. You will give them different Department values so you can see why the Finance rule includes one user and leaves the other outside. Complete the subtabs in order.

        ### 1. Set different Department values

        1. In the Admin Console, open **Directory → People**. Open your first test user's record.
        2. Select **Profile → Edit**, set **Department** to `Lab-Finance`, and save. Do the same for the second test user with `Lab-Operations`.
        3. Reopen both profiles and verify their stored values. Use those exact values in the rules below. If a field is unavailable or read-only, check that you opened an Okta-managed test user with the standard **User** profile.

        ### 2. Create two Okta groups

        1. Open **Directory → Groups**. On **All**, select **Add group**.
        2. Create `LAB-Manual`. For the description, enter **Manual membership practice**.
        3. Create `LAB-Finance`. Use **Group rule practice** for its description.
        4. Open each group and check **People**. Starting with empty groups lets you see which action adds a member.

        The **People** tab is inside an individual group. The built-in **Everyone** group below shows the layout. For this task, open **LAB-Manual**.

        <img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," width="950" height="275" alt="Directory sidebar and Everyone group with the People tab">

        ### 3. Add one user manually

        1. Open `LAB-Manual` and select **Assign people**.
        2. Find the second test user by username. Select **Assign** beside that user, then select **Done**.
        3. Open **People** in `LAB-Manual` and verify that only that test user is a member. Look for **Manually** in the membership information. Use the person's row to verify the change while the directory's summary count catches up.

        ### 4. Compare membership with profile data

        Open the second test user's **Profile** again. The department is still `Lab-Operations` even though you added the user to a group. Return to `LAB-Manual → People` to see the membership. You changed the relationship to the group in Task 3. The profile value is stored on the user record.

    === "2. Rules and membership changes"

        ### 5. Create the department rule

        Open **Rules** on the Groups list. This tab is separate from the **People** tab inside a group.

        <img src="data:image/jpeg;base64," width="950" height="229" alt="Directory sidebar and Groups page showing All and Rules">

        1. Open **Directory → Groups → Rules** and select **Add Rule**.
        2. Name it `LAB-Finance-by-Department`. Under **IF**, choose **Use basic condition**, select **Department**, choose the equality operator, and enter `Lab-Finance`.
        3. In **Then Assign to**, select `LAB-Finance`. Leave the exception list empty and save the rule.
        4. Find the rule in the list. It starts **Inactive**. Open `LAB-Finance → People` and verify that the rule has yet to add either test user.

        ### 6. Activate the rule and verify both outcomes

        1. Return to **Directory → Groups → Rules**. On the line for `LAB-Finance-by-Department`, open **Actions → Activate** and confirm if prompted.
        2. Open `LAB-Finance → People`. Look for the first test user, whose profile says `Lab-Finance`. The second user should stay outside the group.
        3. If the membership does not appear immediately, refresh after processing. If it still differs from what you expect, check the rule is **Active**, the target group is correct, the test user is active, and the stored Department value matches exactly.

        ### 7. Test a move into and out of the group

        1. Open the second user's **Profile**, change **Department** to `Lab-Finance`, and save. Verify that both users now appear in `LAB-Finance`.
        2. Change the second user's Department back to `Lab-Operations`. Refresh the group after processing and verify that the second user no longer appears there.
        3. Open `LAB-Manual → People`. The second user should still be there because you assigned that membership separately. Keep both groups for the next lab.

        ### 8. Test an equivalent expression in a separate group

        1. Create a new Okta group named `LAB-Finance-Expression`. Open **Directory → Groups → Rules → Add Rule**.
        2. Name the rule `LAB-Finance-Expression`. Under **IF**, choose **Use Okta Expression Language (advanced)** and enter `user.department == "Lab-Finance"`.
        3. Set **Then Assign to** to the new `LAB-Finance-Expression` group. Save and activate the rule. Confirm the first user appears in both Finance groups and the second appears in neither.
        4. To see an exception in action, open the **People** tab of `LAB-Finance-Expression` and remove the first test user from that group only. Go to **Directory → Groups → Rules**. On the expression rule only, select **Actions → Deactivate**, then **Actions → Edit**. Inspect **Except The following users**. Okta records the removed user there. Close the editor and reactivate the expression rule to leave it in use with the exception in place. The first user should still be in `LAB-Finance`, which is managed by its own rule.

    === "3. One source and two targets"

        Keep these groups separate from the Finance groups used later in the course. Use the two active test users from the earlier tabs.

        ### 9. Send one source membership to two targets

        1. In **Directory → Groups**, create `LAB-Rule-Source`, `LAB-Rule-Target-A`, and `LAB-Rule-Target-B`. Add the first active test user manually to the source group. Leave both targets empty.
        2. In **Groups → Rules → Add Rule**, name the rule `LAB-Source-to-Two-Targets`. Under the basic **IF** condition, select the group membership condition and choose `LAB-Rule-Source`. If your editor offers the advanced expression instead, use `isMemberOfGroupName("LAB-Rule-Source")` with the unique lab group name.
        3. Add both target groups under **Then Assign to**, save, and activate. Open **People** in each target. The first active test user should appear in both. The second test user should stay outside both.

        ### 10. Trace an update back to the source

        1. Remove the first test user from **LAB-Rule-Source → People**. Refresh both target groups after the rule has processed the change. In this setup, the user should leave both targets because the rule was their only path in.
        2. Add the user back to the source and verify that both target memberships return. If only one appears, open the rule and check that both targets are selected. If neither appears, check the source group's **People** tab, rule status, and exceptions.

    === "4. Multiple sources with OR and AND"

        Keep using the rule from Task 9. Using one rule lets you see the effect of changing just its **IF** condition. Make every membership change in the source groups so you can observe the targets without creating user exceptions.

        ### 11. Add a second source and a third target

        1. In **Directory → Groups → Add group**, create two Okta groups. `LAB-Rule-Source-B` is the second group the rule will check. `LAB-Rule-Target-C` is a third group the rule will assign. Leave the new target empty.
        2. Keep the first test user in the original source group, `LAB-Rule-Source`. Open **LAB-Rule-Source-B → People → Assign people** and add only the second test user. Each user should be in exactly one source.
        3. In **Directory → Groups → Rules → Add Rule**, enter a temporary name such as `LAB-Basic-Preview`. Under **IF → Use basic condition → Group membership**, select both sources. Read **includes any of the following** beside the picker. Under **Then Assign to**, select the three lab targets. In **Preview**, select the first test user, who belongs only to the original source. Confirm **User matches rule**. Try the second user, who belongs only to the second source. They should match too. Select **Cancel** to close the preview without saving another rule.
        4. Open each source group and copy its group ID from the end of the address in your browser. Keep track of which ID belongs to which group. [Okta · Find the group ID](https://support.okta.com/help/s/article/how-to-find-group-ids-through-the-okta-user-interface)

        ### 12. Test a rule where either source is enough

        1. In **Directory → Groups → Rules**, find `LAB-Source-to-Two-Targets`. Select **Actions → Deactivate**, then **Actions → Edit**. Switch **IF** to **Use Okta Expression Language (advanced)** and paste the expression below with your actual source group IDs.

            ```text
            isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_A_ID") OR isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_B_ID")
            ```

        2. Under **Then Assign to**, keep the first two targets and add `LAB-Rule-Target-C`. Preview both users if the editor shows **Preview**. Save and activate. After Okta processes the change, open **People** in all three targets. Both users should appear because each belongs to a source group.
        3. Add the first user to the second source as well. Remove them from the original source and check that they stay in all three targets. Now remove them from the second source. They should leave all three after processing. The second test user should remain in all three.

        ### 13. Test a rule where both sources are required

        1. Add the first user to both sources. Leave the second user in only `LAB-Rule-Source-B`. Deactivate and edit the same rule. Change `OR` to `AND` in **IF**, keep all three targets, save, and activate.
        2. Check **People** in all three targets once processing finishes. The first user should appear. The second should now be outside all three.
        3. Move the second user from B to A and confirm that the result is still outside all three. Remove the first user from either source and confirm that the first user also leaves the targets. For an **AND** rule, one missing membership is enough to make **IF** false.

        ### 14. Mix a group condition with a profile condition

        1. Verify that both test users belong to at least one source. In **Directory → People → Profile**, check that the first user's **Department** is `Lab-Finance` and the second user's is `Lab-Operations`.
        2. Deactivate and edit the same rule. Replace its condition below, using your IDs. Keep the targets, save, and activate.

            ```text
            (isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_A_ID") OR isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_B_ID")) AND user.department == "Lab-Finance"
            ```

        3. Check that only the first user joins the targets. Change the first user's Department temporarily to `Lab-Operations` and verify that they leave the targets even though their source membership is unchanged. Restore `Lab-Finance` and verify that the target memberships return. The Department change can also affect the separate Finance rule from earlier in this lesson.

        ### 15. Exclude everyone in one source group

        1. Put both test users in the original source. Also add the second test user to `LAB-Rule-Source-B`. Keep the first user out of B.
        2. Deactivate and edit the same rule. Use this condition with your group IDs, then save and activate.

            ```text
            isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_A_ID") AND !isMemberOfGroup("SOURCE_B_ID")
            ```

        3. Check all three targets. The first user should qualify. The second should stay outside because they belong to B. Remove the second user from B while leaving them in A. Check that they now appear in all three targets. This group-based exclusion follows membership in B as it changes.

    === "5. Account status and membership"

        Use the second active test user and one disposable staged user for this comparison.

        ### 16. Compare an active user with a staged user

        1. In **Directory → People**, add a disposable Okta-managed user with **Activate later**, following [Lesson 2](02-users-profiles-and-activation.md). Check that the status is **Staged**. Set **Department** to `Lab-Rule-Status` on that user and on the second active test user. Record the second user's original value before changing it.
        2. Create an empty group called `LAB-Rule-Active-Only`. In **Groups → Rules → Add Rule**, choose **Use Okta Expression Language (advanced)** and enter:

            ```text
            user.department == "Lab-Rule-Status" AND user.getInternalProperty("status") == "ACTIVE"
            ```

        3. Select **LAB-Rule-Active-Only** as the target. Save and activate the rule. Open the group's **People** tab and compare it with the two user profiles. Both have the expected Department. Only the active test user should appear in the group.

        ### 17. Verify the rule after activation

        1. Activate the disposable account and complete any required activation steps until **People** shows **Active**. Check the target group after the rule processes the change. If you still see only one member, check the staged user's current status and exact Department value. To trigger a profile update once the account is active, change Department to a temporary value, save, then restore `Lab-Rule-Status` and save again.
        2. Restore the second user's original Department. Clear the lab Department value on the disposable user, then verify that both users leave **LAB-Rule-Active-Only**. Each membership depends on the rule condition.

    === "6. Edit and reactivate a rule"

        ### 18. Change a rule condition and verify the result

        1. Use the active `LAB-Finance-Expression` rule from Task 8. In **Rules**, open **Actions** and find **View** and **Deactivate**. Check that the rule targets the dedicated `LAB-Finance-Expression` group. The original Finance rule remains available for the next lesson.
        2. Deactivate the expression rule and confirm **Inactive**. Choose **Actions → Edit** and change the condition to `user.department == "Lab-Operations"`. Keep the target group and the exception from Task 8. Save and activate.
        3. After processing, check `LAB-Finance-Expression → People`. Expect the second test user, whose Department is `Lab-Operations`, to appear. The first test user should stay outside. Check the saved Department, rule status, target, and exceptions if the result differs.
        4. Deactivate the expression rule again. Before editing, open **People** in the expression group and check that the second user's existing membership is still there. Return to **Rules → Actions → Edit** and restore `user.department == "Lab-Finance"`. Save and activate. Verify the second user leaves the expression group and the first user's exception still applies. Check that the first user still belongs to the original `LAB-Finance` group.
